newsitem.title: CHINA: China state grain fund needed for stable market.
newsitem.headline: China state grain fund needed for stable market.

text.p: China needs an anti-risk fund for state grain purchasers because its commodity hedging instruments are not yet sophisticated enough to provide that security, economists said on Tuesday.
"They don't have very developed commodity options markets to provide that kind of hedging, so they have to go direct," said Shan Li, executive director at Goldman Sachs.

China was mulling creation of an anti-risk fund for state grain buyers and was building more grain warehouses to try and encourage buying of surplus grain, the official China Daily newspaper said on Sunday.

Farmers were protected from grain price fluctuations by a state-set minimum level and mandatory government buying. But state buyers were often reluctant to buy surplus grain for fear of incurring losses later as prices fell, the report said.
The fund would help state purchasers offset possible losses if sales became slack, it said.
The Agricultural Bank of China had arranged US$7.3 billion in loans for state buyers, the report said.
"The only merit is to avoid volatility," said Joe Zhang, senior economist for North Asia at Credit Lyonnais Securities (Asia) Ltd.
"It's like saying we know you're going to make a loss, we don't know how much, this may or may not be enough, but some preparation is necessary," he said.
The government was forced to invest so much in its agricultural sector because of its fear of inflation, the economists said.
"The government simply cannot afford to hurt farmers' incentives for planting," said Vanessa Yeung, senior economist at GK Goh Securities (Hong Kong) Limited.
Should farmers' planting incentive drop, crop production would plunge, raising the inflation bogey again.
China's agricultural policy was caught in a double bind.

On one hand, the government had to continue its tight inflation policy. With food prices in China weighing in at about 40 percent of the inflation basket, this means huge agricultural production must be kept up to keep prices down.
"In order to provide incenctive for farmers, the government has to maintain procurement prices but the market price is dropping because of large supplies," said Yeung.
"The outcome is that the government is increasing subsidies to farmers and imposing a financial burden on itself," she said.
In 1993 and 1994, China had to clamp down on stock and property markets and many commodity exchanges, which provided just such hedging facilities, because of uncontrolled speculation.
But with inflation under tight control, China could pursue other urgently-needed reforms it had held back on, Yeung said.
And as part of continued financial reform, now that the inflation threat had receded China may well revive commodity exchanges, she noted.
Shan Li from Goldman Sachs agreed that measures like an anti-risk fund for state grain buyers were probably temporary.
China's retail inflation in the first half of the year was a year-on-year 1.8 percent, down from 6.1 percent a year ago.
